body.p: Almost every scary headline about infant sleep comes down to the sleep environment — and the environment is one of the few things entirely in your control. Set it up once, correctly, and every single sleep after that is safer on autopilot, no willpower required at 3 AM.

{name} sleeps safest Alone, on the Back, in a Crib. Alone means the crib holds a baby and nothing else — no blankets, pillows, bumpers, stuffed animals or positioners. Back means every sleep, naps included, until the first birthday. Crib means a firm, flat surface with a fitted sheet — a crib, bassinet or portable play yard that meets safety standards.

Keeping the crib or bassinet in your room for at least the first six months is commonly recommended: it makes night feeds easier and is associated with lower sleep-related risk. Sharing a room is protective; sharing an adult bed is where risk climbs — soft mattresses, loose bedding and tired adults are a bad combination for a newborn.

body.h: Dress for the room, not the season
body.p: Overheating is the quiet risk people miss. Aim for a room that feels comfortable to a lightly dressed adult and put {name} in one more light layer than you would wear — a sleep sack instead of a blanket does the job. Check warmth on the chest or the back of the neck; hands and feet always run cool and will mislead you.

The most dangerous place for a newborn to sleep is on a couch or armchair with an exhausted adult. If you're fading during a night feed, put {name} down in the crib first — a crying baby in a safe crib is a far better outcome than two people asleep on a sofa.

Strip the crib to mattress and fitted sheet. Move it into your room if it isn't there. Set the thermostat, pick the sleep sack. Done — you've just made every night of the next year meaningfully safer.
In week one the diaper is the most honest dashboard you have: it reports intake and hydration without a single lab test. Learning to read it buys real peace of mind.

Days 1–2 bring meconium — black-green, tarry, oddly proud of itself. Days 3–4 shift to greenish-brown transitional stools. By day 5 or so: yellow, seedy and loose for breastfed babies, tan and pastier for formula. All of it is on schedule.

Rough guide: about as many wet diapers as days of age until day five, then six or more wets per 24 hours. Stools vary wildly — several a day or one every few days can both be fine once feeding is established.
No wet diaper in 8+ hours, brick-red dust after day four (urate crystals are common only in the first days), white or clay-colored stool, or blood — same-day pediatrician call.
Two taps per change in the tracker and the counting happens by itself — the weekly totals answer half the questions before you ask them.
The umbilical stump is drying leftover tissue — it darkens, shrivels and typically falls off within one to three weeks. Until then it needs almost nothing from you, which is the entire art of it.

body.h: Keep it dry, keep it out of the way
body.p: Fold the diaper below the stump, stick to sponge baths, and let air do the work. The old alcohol-swab ritual is no longer routinely recommended — dry care is the commonly advised approach.
A slightly funky smell near the end and a few drops of blood when it detaches are commonly seen. Resist the urge to help it off — it leaves on its own schedule.
Redness spreading on the surrounding skin, active oozing or pus, a foul strong odor, or fever 100.4°F+ — call your pediatrician the same day.
A tiny raw spot heals in days; a persistent moist pink nub (granuloma) is a quick, painless fix at the office. Then: bathtub officially open.

A yellow tint to the skin and eyes shows up in most newborns — it's usually the single most googled thing in week two. The cause is bilirubin, a normal byproduct of replacing the extra red blood cells babies are born with. A brand-new liver simply needs a few days to catch up with the workload.

Physiological jaundice commonly appears on day 2–3, peaks around days 3–5, and fades by the end of week two. It typically starts at the face and moves down the body as levels rise — which is exactly why the follow-the-yellow check matters more than the shade itself.

Bilirubin leaves the body through stool, which means the everyday fix is unglamorous: frequent feeds. Every feed is literally flushing the yellow out. If {name} is feeding 8–12 times a day and producing wet and dirty diapers on schedule, the system is working.

Call your pediatrician today if the yellow spreads below the knees, deepens after day five, or comes with a sleepy baby who's hard to wake or feeding poorly. Yellow visible in the first 24 hours of life is always checked immediately. None of these calls are overreacting — bilirubin is measured with a quick painless test, and treatment (light therapy) is routine and effective.
Sunlight through a window is not a treatment plan — it's unreliable and risks overheating. Sugar water isn't either. Feed, count diapers, watch the spread, and let the pediatrician own the numbers.

Jaundice is the most common newborn condition there is, and the overwhelming majority of cases resolve with nothing but time and milk. Your job isn't to fix it — it's to feed and to notice. Both are things you're already doing.

articles.title: The weight math of week two

body.p: Newborns commonly lose up to about 7–10% of birth weight in the first days — mostly fluid — and regain it by around two weeks. The dip terrifies parents and rarely surprises pediatricians.
Babies are born pre-loaded with extra fluid for the transition while milk supply ramps up. The scale reads that handoff, not a feeding failure.
The trend and the diapers. Regular feeds, six-plus wets a day and steady stools say intake is working better than any single weigh-in — home scales mislead more than they help.

That checkup exists largely for this: confirming baby is back to birth weight or clearly heading there. If not, the pediatrician adjusts the feeding plan with you — it's a fixable logistics problem, not a verdict.
Fewer wet diapers, a sleepy baby who's hard to wake for feeds, or feeding refusal — don't wait for the scheduled visit.
While the stump is attached, sponge baths keep it dry: warm room, warm water, baby on a towel, one zone at a time while the rest stays wrapped.

body.h: You need less than the aisle sold you
body.p: Warm water handles most of a newborn. A drop of mild fragrance-free cleanser for the diaper zone and folds is plenty; two to three baths a week is commonly enough — newborn skin dries out with more.
Neck creases, armpits, thigh folds — milk and lint collect there. Pat dry thoroughly; moisture trapped in folds is how irritation starts.

Hand on the baby always, everything within reach before you start, water comfortable to your inner wrist. A crying baby mid-bath is normal; a slippery baby with your supplies across the room is the situation to avoid.
Once the stump is off and healed, the real (tiny) bathtub opens — same rules, more splashing.

articles.title: Cluster feeding: is she getting enough?

body.p: Feeding every 30–60 minutes for a stretch of the evening is one of the most commonly seen patterns of the first weeks — and the most commonly misread. The fear is always the same: my supply is failing. Usually the opposite is happening: {name} is placing a bulk order, and the factory is adjusting production.

Milk production runs on demand signals. More frequent nursing tells the body to make more; the cluster IS the mechanism, not evidence of its failure. Growth spurts around weeks 2–3 and 6 commonly bring a day or two of near-constant feeding, then everything settles at the new volume.

You can't see ounces at the breast, but you can count what comes out. From day five onward, roughly six or more wet diapers per 24 hours plus regular stools is the commonly used sign that intake is fine. Weight checks at pediatric visits confirm the trend. Those two numbers beat any amount of worrying at 11 PM.

body.h: What fussiness at the breast doesn't mean
body.p: Pulling off, fussing and re-latching in the evening is commonly seen and usually reflects tiredness and an immature nervous system winding down — not an empty breast. Evening milk also flows slower, which frustrated little customers make loudly known.

Set up a feeding station before the evening shift: water, snacks, phone charger, remote. Hand off everything that isn't feeding. If bottle-feeding, the same clustering happens — follow the appetite in smaller, more frequent servings rather than pushing bigger bottles.

Fewer wet diapers than expected, no return to birth weight by the two-week visit, or feeding that seems painful or ineffective — those go to the pediatrician or a lactation consultant. Everything else is a newborn doing newborn math.
Spit-up dribbles or rolls out effortlessly, often with a burp, and the baby barely notices. Vomiting is forceful, distressing and usually repeated. The first is laundry; the second is information.

The valve at the top of a newborn stomach is lazy for months. Commonly seen: spitting after many feeds, with volume that looks bigger on your shirt than it really was. Happy, gaining babies who spit are called 'happy spitters' in clinics for a reason.
Upright 15–20 minutes after feeds, unhurried burping, avoid bouncing right after eating, and check the bottle nipple flow if bottle-feeding. None of it eliminates spit-up; all of it reduces it.

Forceful projectile vomiting after multiple feeds in a row, green or yellow-stained vomit, blood, a baby who seems in pain, or fewer wet diapers — pediatrician now, these are different stories from spit-up.
Spit-up commonly peaks around 2–4 months and fades as sitting and solids arrive. The washing machine sees the worst of it, not the baby.
Milia (tiny white dots), baby acne, flaky peeling, erythema toxicum (blotchy red spots with pale centers that migrate) — week three skin runs a rotating show of harmless-looking harmless things.
Almost all of it resolves on its own. No scrubbing, no squeezing, no acne products, no heavy lotions on the face. Warm water and patience outperform every product for these.
Yellowish scales on the scalp — commonly seen for months. A soft brush during baths, optionally a little plain oil before, lifts flakes gently. It doesn't itch or bother the owner.
Frequent changes, pat dry, air time, and a zinc barrier cream at the first sign of redness — prevention is nearly the whole game.
Blisters or pus-filled bumps, a rash plus fever 100.4°F+, raw bleeding areas, or a rash that makes the baby miserable — those are pediatrician territory, same day.

articles.title: The crying curve has a shape

body.h: The most useful graph in parenting
body.p: Newborn crying isn't random — it follows a curve. Total daily crying commonly starts climbing around two weeks, peaks near two months, and eases substantially by three to four months. Knowing the shape changes everything: the loud stretch has an end date, and you're allowed to count down to it.

Here is the part nobody says out loud: at this age, some crying has no findable cause. Fed, dry, warm, held — still crying. This is a documented feature of normal newborn development, not a verdict on your parenting. Babies in every culture on the planet do this, on roughly the same schedule.

Work a loop instead of hunting the one magic fix: feed if it's been a while, fresh diaper, motion (walking, rocking, stroller), sound (shushing, white noise), sucking (breast, pacifier), skin contact, a change of scenery to a dimmer room. Any one of them may work today and fail tomorrow. That's normal too.

Never shake a baby — not from frustration, not 'to snap them out of it'. If the crying has drained you to the edge, put {name} down safely in the crib, walk into another room, breathe for a few minutes. A crying baby in a safe crib is fine. A parent at their breaking point needs the break more than the baby needs holding right that second. Hand off to a partner the moment one exists.

A cry that sounds unlike your baby — high-pitched, weak, moaning — or crying with fever, vomiting, refusal to feed or a bulging soft spot: call your pediatrician now. Inconsolable crying for hours despite feeding and holding deserves the same call.
It rises, it peaks, it falls. You're not doing anything wrong. It has an end date.
Immature gut, air swallowed while feeding and crying, a digestive system running its first month of production — gas is commonly the background noise of month one, loud in every sense.

Bicycle legs, knees-to-tummy holds, tummy time (pressure helps), a warm bath, and carrying baby face-down along your forearm — the classic rotation. Different babies vote for different moves; run the loop.

Mid-feed burp plus end-of-feed burp, trying more than one position (shoulder, sitting supported, face-down on lap). Bottle-feeding: check nipple flow and keep the bottle angled so the nipple stays full of milk, not air.
Simethicone drops are popular and considered low-risk, but evidence they beat placebo is thin — ask your pediatrician before adding anything, and skip 'gripe waters' with unclear ingredients.

Grunting, squirming and dramatic faces with normal feeding and weight gain — commonly just gas. Inconsolable crying for hours, vomiting, blood in stool or fever — that's a call, not a bicycle session.
Sucking soothes — it's a genuine self-regulation tool. And pacifier use at sleep time is associated with reduced sleep-related risk, which is why safe-sleep guidance treats it kindly.

Introduced too early it can muddy breastfeeding (commonly suggested: wait until nursing is established, around 3–4 weeks); it can become a night-waking accessory when it falls out; and years down the road, prolonged use matters for teeth — a problem for a much older child, not this one.
Offer at sleep, don't force, never coat it in anything sweet, no clips or strings in the crib, and if it falls out mid-sleep — it doesn't need reinserting unless baby objects.
Commonly seen and completely fine — the pacifier is optional equipment, not a requirement. Some babies find their fist instead; same tool, always attached.
Families run happily with and without. Pick based on your baby's temperament and your feeding situation, not on internet debates.

The late-afternoon fussy stretch — feeding, fussing, dozing, waking, repeat — is so commonly seen it has a folk name. It tends to show up around weeks 2–3 and fade by 3–4 months, running right alongside the crying curve's climb.

By day's end an immature nervous system has absorbed hours of light, sound, faces and sensations with no off switch. The evening meltdown is commonly the sound of an overstimulated system trying to power down — which is why the fixes that work are mostly about turning the world down.
Start dimming before the storm: lights low from late afternoon, screens off near the baby, visitors wrapped up, one calm room. A dark, boring environment isn't neglect — at this hour it's medicine.

The classic combo for the fussy hours: baby in a carrier, parent walking, white noise on. Contact regulates a newborn's system better than any gadget; the carrier gives your arms and back a fighting chance. A stroller loop outside or even standing and swaying counts.

Cluster feeding and witching hour overlap heavily. Offering the breast or bottle again 40 minutes after the last feed is fine — comfort feeding in the evening is commonly seen and doesn't 'spoil' anything or ruin the schedule that doesn't exist yet.

If there are two of you, split the evening into 45-minute shifts with a hard handoff — a known end time makes the loud stretch survivable. Solo tonight? Lower every other bar: dinner is cereal, dishes wait, the only job is the two of you getting to 10 PM.
The womb was loud — a constant whoosh louder than a vacuum cleaner. Steady noise recreates the familiar sound floor and masks household spikes that startle a light sleeper.

Volume and distance: keep the machine across the room (not in or on the crib) and the level moderate — around the loudness of a soft shower, not a hair dryer. If you have to raise your voice over it, it's too loud.
Plain steady noise through the sleep period commonly works better than sounds that shift or stop — the change itself can wake a baby surfacing between cycles.

Needing noise to sleep isn't a character flaw or a trap: it's a portable, cheap sleep association — far easier to travel with than most alternatives. Wean later by lowering volume gradually, if you ever care to.
Hunger, an overtired baby or the 5 PM witching hour. It's a background helper, not a sleep strategy on its own.
Sneezing without a cold, hiccuping daily, snorty breathing, occasional irregular rhythms with brief pauses — the newborn respiratory system is loud and commonly completely fine.
Tiny nasal passages plus lint, milk drops and dust equal frequent resets. Sneezing is the built-in nose-cleaning program, not illness.
Commonly seen daily, often after feeds, and they bother parents far more than babies. They fade on their own; a few minutes upright or a brief suck usually shortens the show.
For true congestion: a drop or two of saline, wait a moment, then a gentle bulb or snot-sucker before feeds and sleep. That's the entire toolkit for a stuffy newborn — no decongestants at this age.

Working hard to breathe (ribs pulling in, nostrils flaring, grunting each breath), blue tint around lips, pauses over 10 seconds, or refusing feeds because breathing is hard — emergency evaluation, don't wait.

articles.title: The first smile is a conversation

body.p: Around six to eight weeks, the smile changes category: it starts happening in response to you — your face, your voice, your ridiculous sound effects. That's the social smile, one of the earliest milestones on the CDC's two-month list, and the first time communication flows both directions on purpose.

Development at this age runs on a simple loop researchers call serve-and-return: baby serves (a look, a coo, a smile), you return (eye contact, words, a smile back), repeat. Every loop is a rep for the social brain. You don't need flashcards or apps — you are the enrichment program.

Narrate the day in that sing-song voice that comes naturally — it exists in every language and babies measurably prefer it. Pause after you speak, as if waiting for an answer. Long before words, {name} is learning the deepest rule of language: we take turns.

The 8-to-12-inch range where newborn vision is sharpest is exactly feeding distance — nature's design for face study. During calm awake windows, get close, make slow expressions, hold eye contact. Watching {name} watch you is the whole curriculum.

Milestone windows are wide. Some babies smile socially at five weeks, some at nine or ten. Worth mentioning at the two-month checkup: no social smiling, no calming to your voice, or no response to loud sounds. Mentioning is not diagnosing — it's how checkups are supposed to work.
The payoff era begins here: after weeks of one-way service, the customer starts tipping. Take the videos. Future you says thank you.

body.h: For the babies who file complaints
body.p: Plenty of babies protest floor tummy time at first — the position is heavy work. Protest doesn't cancel the program; it changes the format.
Tummy on your chest while you recline, tummy across your lap, football carry face-down, side-lying play — all build related strength. Start where tolerance is, migrate floorward over weeks.
Right after a diaper change (not straight after a big feed), your face at eye level, one interesting object, short sessions before tiredness. End on a small win, not at the meltdown.
Total daily minutes beat session length: six two-minute rounds equal one heroic twelve-minute battle — with far fewer tears on both sides.
If head-lifting shows no progress across weeks, or baby strongly favors turning to one side only — bring it up at the next visit; early positional issues are very fixable.

A previously settled baby suddenly feeds constantly, sleeps oddly and wants holding around the clock — for two or three days. Commonly seen around weeks 2–3, 6, and 3 months, though babies read different calendars.
Rapid growth demands calories, and frequent feeding is the ordering system: demand tells supply to scale. The clinginess is part of the same package — growth is disorganizing work.
Feed on demand, lower the ambition level, hydrate and snack yourself if breastfeeding, and treat the stretch as weather: real, temporary, not caused by anything you did.
A spurt keeps the diaper counts normal and resolves within days at a new baseline. Falling wet counts, feeding refusal, fever or a baby who seems unwell — different story, pediatrician call.
Your tracker makes spurts visible: feed frequency jumps, then settles. Watching the pattern resolve on a chart is oddly reassuring at 4 AM.

Because back-sleeping is non-negotiable for safety, awake time on the tummy is where neck, shoulder and core strength get built — the muscles behind rolling, sitting, crawling and a nicely rounded head shape. Think of it as the gym membership that comes with back-sleeping.

body.h: Little and often beats long and miserable
body.p: Forget the image of a 20-minute session. Two to five minutes, several times a day, from the early weeks — that's the commonly recommended pattern. Right after a diaper change (not straight after a big feed) is a natural slot. Total minutes across the day matter more than any single stretch.

A firm blanket on the floor, you down at eye level, a high-contrast card or a baby-safe mirror within view. Your face is the best toy in the room — most babies work hardest at head-lifting when the reward is looking at you.

Plenty of babies protest the floor at first. Legit alternatives that count: tummy-to-chest while you recline, tummy across your lap, football-hold carrying. Start there, migrate floorward as tolerance grows. A few tears at the start are normal; escalate to a break, not a battle.
Tummy time is an awake, supervised activity — the moment sleepiness wins, baby goes to the crib and onto the back. The pairing is the whole system: back to sleep, tummy to play.
Week by week: brief head lifts, then steadier holds, then chin and chest up on forearms around two to three months. Log it in Activity and the trend line will surprise you.

Back-sleeping is non-negotiable for safety — and it means the back of the head logs serious surface hours. Mild flattening (positional plagiocephaly) is commonly seen and mostly cosmetic and reversible at this age.
Alternate which end of the crib baby's head points each night, switch carrying arms, move the play mat relative to the light — babies turn toward interesting things, and the turning is the therapy.
Every awake minute off the back of the head counts double: strength program and pressure relief in one. Supervised side-lying play counts too.
Car seats, bouncers and swings all press the same spot. Use them for transport and short breaks, not as default real estate — floor beats container for both head and hips.

Noticeable asymmetry, a strong preference to look one way (possible tight neck muscle — very treatable), or flattening that seems to progress — раise at the next checkup; early intervention is simple, late is harder.

articles.title: Small maintenance: nails and cradle cap

body.p: Newborn nails grow fast, are soft and scratch-capable. File during sleep with a soft baby file, or clip when hands are milk-drunk limp — press the fingertip pad away from the nail and clip the white edge only.
Every parent does it once. Rinse, press briefly with clean gauze — no adhesive bandages (they're a choking risk when sucked off). Forgive yourself; the finger already has.
Yellow scales on the scalp: soft brush during the bath, optionally a small amount of plain oil 15 minutes before to loosen. It's not itchy, not contagious, not a hygiene verdict.
Cotton swabs never go inside anything: wipe outer ears only, clean eye corners with damp cotton from inner corner outward, and let sneezes run the nose department.
Redness around a nail, discharge from an eye that keeps returning, or cradle cap spreading to face and body with irritation — quick pediatrician questions, all easily handled.

body.h: What the two-month visit looks like
body.p: Measurements, a development check against the two-month milestones, your questions — and the first big round of routine vaccines. It's usually the visit parents dread most and, in hindsight, the one that goes more smoothly than imagined.

You're not just allowed to comfort during the shots — it measurably helps. Feeding during or right after, skin contact, and your calm voice all reduce distress. Ask to hold {name} during the injections; most offices are set up for exactly that.

Commonly seen afterwards: extra sleepiness, mild fussiness, a little less appetite, tenderness at the injection sites — for a day or so. Plan a quiet day. Extra holding and extra feeds are the whole recovery protocol most babies need.

Fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher in a baby under three months is always a same-day call, vaccine day or not. Also call for crying that stays inconsolable for three or more hours, or anything that simply worries you — the after-hours line exists for exactly this. Don't give fever medicine to a newborn unless the pediatrician tells you to.

The visit is your dedicated slot with the pediatrician — spend it. Bring the questions saved in Ask, the feeding and sleep patterns from your logs, and anything from Worth watching you've been sitting on. Real data beats memory at 9 AM after a broken night.

The schedule {name} is on reflects decades of safety monitoring across millions of children. Vaccine day is a milestone of its own — you're doing the protective thing, even when it comes with fifteen loud seconds.

articles.title: After the shots: a reading guide

body.p: Commonly seen in the 24–48 hours after two-month vaccines: extra sleepiness, mild fussiness, reduced appetite, tenderness or a small firm bump at injection sites. All of it says the immune system took the assignment.

More holding, more feeds, a quiet day. The site bump can last a couple of weeks and needs nothing. Don't pre-dose fever medicine 'just in case' — give it only if your pediatrician advises for actual discomfort.
Under three months, 100.4°F (38°C) or higher is always a same-day call — vaccine day or not. Measure rectally for accuracy at this age; forehead strips underperform exactly when it matters.
Inconsolable crying beyond three hours, limpness or unresponsiveness, hives or facial swelling, or anything your gut flags as wrong — call. Serious reactions are rare; asking is always free.
Note in Medicine what happened and when — the pattern makes the four-month round predictable instead of scary.

Somewhere around now, the postpartum visit happens — and it's commonly the most-skipped appointment in the family. Baby has had several checkups already; the person who did the delivering deserves one that counts.

Physical recovery, bleeding patterns, blood pressure, incision or tear healing, contraception timing — and, just as centrally, mood. Screening for postpartum depression and anxiety is a standard part, not an accusation.

Pain that isn't fading, leaking urine, pain with intimacy, headaches, feelings that scare you or a persistent flatness — all of it is treatable and all of it belongs on the list. The check-in log in this app can jog your memory of how the weeks actually went.
If most days have felt like running on empty for two weeks or more, that's worth telling a professional now — not at the next scheduled slot. PSI helpline: 1-800-944-4773, free and judgment-free.

body.h: Why this is a baby-care article
body.p: Because the research is blunt: the caregiver's wellbeing is infrastructure for the baby's. Maintenance of the infrastructure is not selfish; it's the job.

articles.title: Coos, squeals and the language project

body.p: Somewhere around now the repertoire expands beyond crying: coos, gurgles, squeals, experimental volume tests. It sounds like noise; it's actually phase one of a language project that runs for years — and you're the co-researcher.

When {name} coos and you coo back, then pause, then wait — that turn-taking loop is the deep structure of every conversation they'll ever have. Babies whose sounds get answered practice more. You're not being silly; you're running the drill.

'Now we're washing hands. Warm water! Now the towel.' Live commentary feels absurd and is exactly right: language grows from hearing real words attached to real moments, thousands of times. No product required — laundry narration is as good as any class.
Reading to a two-month-old isn't about plot. It's rhythm, your voice, page-turning ritual and high-contrast pictures. A board book at this age is a listening exercise — five minutes counts.
Speak both, each parent in whichever feels natural. Growing up around two languages is commonly seen worldwide and isn't confusing — the timeline of babble and first words stays broadly on track.

At the next visit, mention if {name} doesn't react to loud sounds, doesn't quiet to familiar voices, or makes no sounds beyond crying. Hearing gets screened at birth, but noticing at home is a real second layer.

For babies this age, guidance is unusually unanimous: no screen time except video chatting. Not because a glowing rectangle causes instant harm — because every screen minute displaces the serve-and-return interaction that actually builds the brain.
Grandma on a video call counts as interaction, not screen time — there's a live human responding on the other end. Enjoy freely.
A baby glancing at your show while feeding at 2 AM is life, not failure. The guidance targets parked-in-front-of-content time, not ambient household reality.

The trickier effect is 'technoference' — a parent absorbed in the phone misses the baby's serves. No guilt prescribed; just an honest nudge to park the phone for a few fully-present play windows a day. The tracker works in two taps precisely so it doesn't hold you hostage.
Narration, songs, faces, floor time — the boring-sounding program is the evidence-backed one, and you're already running it.

articles.title: Daytime naps: a loose rhythm emerges

body.p: Around now many babies drift from random dozing toward a sketchable day: wake, feed, play, sleepy signs, nap — repeat. It's a rhythm, not a schedule; treat it in pencil.
At this age most babies handle roughly 60–90 minutes awake before needing sleep again. Watch the baby first and the clock second: sleepy cues trump timers.
Four-ish naps of wildly uneven length is commonly seen; a 30-minute cat-nap and a 2-hour marathon in the same day are both normal outputs of an immature sleep system.

Daytime naps in the same safe crib help night sleep learn its address — but stroller and carrier naps keep life livable. Aim the first nap of the day at the crib and let the rest land where the day takes you.

body.h: Let the log do the noticing
body.p: A week of sleep entries will show the pattern before your tired brain does — the stats card assembles the sketch automatically.

Around two to three months many babies start producing one longer night block — four, five, sometimes six hours. If it's happening: enjoy, and don't wake a healthy, gaining baby to feed at night unless your pediatrician said otherwise. If it isn't yet: also normal, the range is wide.

The single most useful night habit: make 2 AM the dullest hour of {name}'s day. Dim light only, whisper voice, no play, no phone flashlight tours. Feed, change if needed, back down. Day gets light and voices; night gets nothing worth waking for.

Mornings near a bright window, normal household noise during naps, daylight walks — versus dim, quiet evenings. You're training the circadian clock with contrast, and at this age light is the main lever you have.

A three-step pre-sleep ritual — feed, sleep sack, same lullaby — repeated nightly becomes a conditioned signal within weeks. It's the cheapest sleep infrastructure you'll ever build, and it pays compound interest through every regression to come.

When the long stretch appears, claim it: go to bed embarrassingly early once or twice a week and put your phone across the room. Ninety unbroken minutes of your own sleep changes the next day more than any productivity trick.

Growth spurts, vaccine days and developmental leaps will bend the nights again — that's traffic, not a wrong turn. The trend across weeks in your sleep stats is the honest scoreboard, not any single rough night.

articles.title: Car seat basics for brief travelers

body.p: Rear-facing infant seat, back seat, harness snug at or below shoulder level, chest clip at armpit height, no bulky jackets between baby and straps. That combination does the heavy lifting of car safety.
After buckling, pinch the strap at the shoulder — if you can gather slack between your fingers, tighten. Snug enough that a coat of webbing hugs, not squeezes.

body.h: Car seats are transport, not real estate
body.p: Sleeping in a moving car is fine and supervised; the risk pattern is the parked seat used as a bed — the semi-upright angle can compromise a young baby's airway. Arrived and asleep? Transfer to the flat crib.
Most seats are installed imperfectly. A certified car seat check (fire stations, hospitals commonly offer free inspections) takes 20 minutes and upgrades your confidence permanently.
Plan feeding stops — take baby out of the seat for feeds; never bottle-prop in the seat. A passenger seat adult companion for the first big drive makes everything calmer.
Two people each getting one protected 4–5 hour block beats two people surviving on shredded 90-minute fragments — same total baby care, dramatically better human function.

The shift split (one parent owns 9 PM–2 AM, the other 2–7 AM); the weekday/weekend split; the feed-vs-everything-else split for breastfeeding families (one feeds, the other handles diaper, resettling, and morning). Pick by feeding setup and chronotypes — the owl takes the late shift.
Off-duty parent sleeps in another room if possible, earplugs allowed, phone away. The block only restores if it's genuinely protected — 'sleeping with one ear open' restores nobody.

If pumping works for you, one expressed bottle buys the feeding parent a real block. If not, the non-feeding parent still owns everything around feeds — bringing baby over, changing, resettling — which commonly halves the feeding parent's awake time.
What worked in week 6 may fail in week 10. A two-minute Sunday check-in ('how are nights actually going for you?') keeps the system honest — the mom check-in card in this app is a decent prompt.

By now {name} broadcasts three main states — hungry, tired, overstimulated — and each has tells that show up before the crying does. Catching cues at the whisper stage instead of the siren stage is the closest thing to a parenting superpower this month.

Rooting toward anything that touches the cheek, hands to mouth, lip smacking, restless head-turning at the chest. Crying is the last hunger cue, not the first — a calm latch beats a frantic one, so feeding at the early signs makes the whole meal easier.

Glazed staring into the distance, losing interest in your face, jerky movements, ear or eye rubbing, a specific whiny pitch. The window between 'sleepy' and 'overtired' is short at this age — a drowsy baby goes down easy, an overtired one fights the very sleep they need.

Turning the face away, arching, splaying fingers, hiccuping or sneezing during play — commonly seen signs of a full sensory tank. The response is subtraction: dimmer room, fewer faces, quiet hold. Looking away from you isn't rejection; it's self-regulation working.

Cues plus data beat either alone. If the log says ninety minutes awake and the whining starts — that's the tired cue confirmed. Two hours since the last feed plus fists in mouth — hunger. The tracker turns guessing into pattern-matching.
Offering food to a tired baby or a nap to a hungry one happens to everyone, daily. Babies are forgiving test audiences — adjust and go again.
Looking away, arching, splayed fingers, hiccups mid-play, fussing that escalates with more entertainment — commonly the signs of a sensory tank at capacity, not boredom.

body.h: Why more fun makes it worse
body.p: The instinct is to add: new toy, bigger smile, louder song. An overstimulated nervous system needs the opposite — every addition is another item on an already overflowing desk.
Dim room, low voice or silence, gentle rocking or stillness, maybe a feed or sucking. Think of it as closing tabs: remove input until the system settles, commonly a few minutes.
Watch for the early cues during play and end sessions on a win. Alternating stimulation and quiet through the day trains self-regulation better than marathon entertainment blocks.
Guests are a common overstimulation source — enthusiastic faces at close range for an hour. Схедule visits for the baby's best window, and let 'she needs a quiet break' be a full sentence.

articles.title: Introducing a bottle to a breastfed baby

body.p: Commonly suggested: after breastfeeding is established (around 3–4 weeks) but before rigid preferences form (by 6–8 weeks it can get harder). Week 11 is still workable — expect a negotiation, not a disaster.
Someone other than the nursing parent offers it (babies smell the original nearby and reasonably hold out), calm-but-hungry timing, slow-flow nipple, milk warmed to body temperature.
Baby fairly upright, bottle horizontal, nipple tickles the lip and baby draws it in, pauses every few minutes — mimics breast rhythm, prevents chugging and keeps the breast competitive.

Commonly seen. Rotate variables one at a time: different person, different position (walking, facing outward), sleepy vs alert timing, different nipple shape. Try once a day without turning it into a battle — pressure teaches refusal.
If a bottle replaces a nursing session regularly, the supply signal drops accordingly — pump near that time if maintaining full supply matters to your plan.

articles.title: The rolling era: a safety sweep

body.p: Somewhere between now and the next few weeks, {name} lands the first roll — usually to their own astonishment, often at the least convenient moment. The trick is to renovate the environment before the skill arrives, not after the first scare.

From now on, no unattended second on changing tables, beds, couches or counters. The first roll is unannounced. One hand on the baby during changes becomes muscle memory; supplies live within arm's reach so you never step away.

If you still swaddle, the first signs of rolling are the hard stop — arms need to be free once flipping is possible. A sleeves-free sleep sack keeps the cozy without the restraint. Same night, no phase-out: this one is a switch, not a dial.

Rolling babies relocate themselves. The bare-crib rule earns its keep now: nothing loose, nothing strung across, nothing within pull-reach from inside — including monitor cords and wall art. Lower the mattress if it's still on the newborn setting.

Keep placing {name} on the back for every sleep. Once babies roll both ways on their own, they may settle where they roll — the job is a completely bare sleep space, not repositioning patrols all night.

The safest playground for a mover is the lowest one. A cleared floor zone — blanket, a couple of toys, no small objects — is where the next six months of motor development actually happen. Do the sweep this week; the deadline sets itself.
Rolling is imminent or here, and rolling is transport. The gap between 'can't move' and 'found the one cable in the room' is commonly a single afternoon.

Get on the floor at baby height and tour the home: outlets at eye level, cords within pull-reach, small objects under furniture, plant pots, bag straps. What you can reach, baby will reach sooner than seems possible.

Outlet covers; cords wrapped and routed high; the coin-sized-object sweep (toilet-roll-tube test: fits through = choking hazard); heavy tippables anchored — bookcases, dressers and the TV; houseplants audited; bags and their contents off the floor.
Fully proof one room as the free-roam zone rather than lightly proofing everything. One genuinely safe room means supervised freedom for baby and an occasional exhale for you.
Stair gates matter at crawling, cabinet locks at cruising. Level one is about the floor world — do it this week, upgrade as mobility upgrades.

articles.title: Dressing for sleep: the sleep sack era

body.p: Loose blankets are off the table for safe sleep, swaddles retire when rolling starts — the wearable blanket is what remains, and it's genuinely better: warmth that can't cover a face or be kicked off.
Sleep sacks come in warmth ratings (TOG). Rough guide: light 0.5–1.0 for warm rooms, 2.5 for cool ones. Room around 68–72°F with a 1.0 sack and one layer underneath is a commonly comfortable default.
Dress baby in one more light layer than you'd wear to sleep in that room — then verify by feel: chest or back of neck should be warm, not sweaty. Cool hands lie; ignore them.
Sweaty neck, damp hair, flushed cheeks — too warm (the riskier direction; overheating matters for safe sleep). Cool chest and fussing at sleep onset — add a layer.
Armholes snug enough that baby can't slide inside the sack; neckline that can't ride over the chin; correct size, not aspirational. Zipper upside-down models win the 3 AM diaper Olympics.

articles.title: The 4-month sleep shift: read this early

body.h: A heads-up, not a horror story
body.p: Sometime in the next month or so, many babies' sleep temporarily gets messier: more night wakings, shorter naps, harder settling. It has a scary nickname online — 'the four-month regression' — but here's the honest reframe: it isn't sleep breaking. It's sleep growing up.

Around this age sleep architecture matures into adult-like cycles, with a light phase every 45–60 minutes. Adults surface from those and dive back without noticing. Babies surface and — depending on what they know — either resettle or call for the settling crew. That's you.

How {name} falls asleep at bedtime is what they expect at every 2 AM surfacing. Practicing drowsy-but-awake at bedtime now — down sleepy but not fully asleep, even succeeding one try in three — is the single highest-leverage preparation. No crying method required; it's just reps.
Dark room (blackout-level), consistent wind-down ritual, white noise if you use it, boring nights protocol. Every basic you cement before the shift is one variable that isn't wobbling during it.

body.h: Plan the logistics like a project
body.p: If it hits, it commonly runs two to six bumpy weeks. Pre-agree night shifts with your partner, lower daytime expectations in advance, and pick ONE approach to night wakings you'll both hold for two weeks before judging — mid-night strategy changes are how everyone ends up more tired.
Post-shift sleep is more mature and, eventually, more consolidated than before. Your sleep stats will show the dip and the recovery — trust the multi-week trend, not Tuesday.

articles.title: Wake windows at the three-month mark

body.p: Awake windows commonly lengthen to about 75–120 minutes around three months — enough for a feed, a proper play block and a wind-down before the tank empties.
Feed at wake-up, active play in the middle (tummy time, tracking games, the floor gym), calming tail end — dimmer, slower, quieter. Loading play early and calm late makes the nap landing smoother.

Fighting sleep with crying and arching commonly means overtired (window ran long); playing happily in the crib for 20 minutes then fussing commonly means undertired (window ran short). Adjust by 10–15 minutes, not by an hour.
The stretch before night sleep commonly runs longest. A consistent wind-down ritual there — feed, sack, song — is the anchor that survives all the coming sleep weather.
Growth days, vaccine days and leaps bend everything. The log's weekly view shows your baby's real windows better than any chart from the internet — including this one.
Measurements and growth curve, the four-month milestone check (head control, pushing up, laughing, hand engagement), feeding review, sleep questions and the second vaccine round.
Your logs answer the standard questions precisely: feeds per day, night stretches, tummy-time minutes. The doctor-visit sets in Ask compile your open questions — export before you go.

Anything sitting in 'Worth watching' cards you weren't sure about; the timing of starting solids for your baby; what the doctor wants to see before the six-month visit; any asymmetry or preference you've noticed.
If the four-month sleep shift has started, describe the pattern in numbers from the log — 'waking every 90 minutes since Tuesday' gets better advice than 'sleep is terrible'.
Log the vaccines in Medicine with any reactions, note the measured weight and length in Measure — your growth history builds itself from here.
